sections.h2: What does the Fulton County Recorder do?
sections.html:
The Fulton County Recorder keeps the permanent public record of who owns land in the county and what liens or mortgages sit on it. The county's own Recorder page describes the job as keeping, safeguarding and organizing every land document so a buyer can be sure of a clear title and a lender can lend against the property.

Fulton County sits west of Toledo and is part of the Toledo metropolitan area. It was created in 1850 from parts of Henry, Lucas and Williams counties. Wauseon became the seat in 1871 after the railroad pulled growth south from Ottokee, and the courthouse there dates to 1872. Every deed for a house in Archbold, Delta, Swanton, Fayette, Lyons, Metamora or Wauseon ends up in the same office.

sections.h2: Where is the Fulton County Recorder's office and when is it open?
sections.html:
The office is in the county building at 152 S. Fulton St., Suite 175, Wauseon, OH 43567. The staff directory lists hours of Monday through Friday, 8:30 am to 4:30 pm, and the phone number is (419) 337-9232.

  • Recorder: Suite 175, where the deed is recorded last.
  • Auditor: Suite 165 in the same building, where the deed is transferred first. The real estate line is (419) 337-9200.
  • Land records search: linked from the county's Records Search page for looking up past deeds and mortgages by name or parcel.

The county site also posts a Real Property Conveyance Standards PDF and printable plats and land surveys on the Recorder page. Pull those before you draft a legal description.

sections.h2: What has to happen before a Fulton County deed can be recorded?
sections.html:
The deed passes through the Auditor before it reaches the Recorder. Fulton County's conveyance standards say the goal is a standard check of every legal description so errors are caught and the parcel is described correctly for tax purposes. Unusual cases go to a group made up of the County Engineer, the Auditor and the Planning Director.

  1. Draft the deed with a legal description that matches the prior deed of record.
  2. Sign it in front of a notary. Ohio's acknowledgment statute, R.C. 5301.01, also allows a judge, court clerk, county auditor, county engineer or mayor to take the acknowledgment.
  3. Take it to the Auditor in Suite 165 for the description check, the conveyance fee and the transfer stamp.
  4. Walk it down to Suite 175 and pay the Recorder's fee.

The statute behind the county transfer tax says the fee is paid to the Auditor before the deed is presented to the Recorder, so keep that order. Ask the Recorder's office what endorsement it wants to see on the deed.

sections.h2: What does the Fulton County Auditor charge to transfer a deed?
sections.html:
Fulton County charges $4.00 per thousand dollars of total consideration, rounded up to the nearest $100, plus $0.50 per parcel for the transfer. The county's own worked example on that page shows consideration of $100,001 being treated as $100,100, with a conveyance fee of $400.40.

Under Ohio law the statement-of-value fee is ten cents per $100 under R.C. 319.54(G)(3), and a county board may levy a further tax of up to thirty cents per $100 under R.C. 322.02. The grantor pays at delivery of the deed, before it is presented to the Recorder.

No fee is charged for some transfers. R.C. 319.54(G)(3) lists them, and the list includes:

  • transfers between husband and wife, or from parent to child, that are gifts;
  • transfers where no money or other valuable consideration changes hands and the deal is not a gift;
  • conveyances among the heirs or devisees of one decedent when no money is paid;
  • a trustee conveying to the grantor of a revocable trust.

If your sale looks like one of these, ask the Auditor's real estate office before you assume the fee applies.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to record a deed in Fulton County?
sections.html:
Recording fees are set by the state and split in half between the basic recording fee and the Ohio Housing Trust Fund. Each printed side of a page counts as one page. A county may add a preservation surcharge of up to $5.00 per document, so ask the Fulton Recorder for the exact total before you mail a check.

sections.h2: What formatting rules does Fulton County enforce on a deed?
sections.html:
Ohio's standard-format statute, R.C. 317.114, applies to the deed you hand the Recorder. A document that misses the rules is still accepted, but it costs an extra ten dollars base fee and ten dollars housing trust fee.

  • Print no smaller than a ten point font.
  • Paper between 8.5 by 11 and 8.5 by 14 inches.
  • Black or blue ink only, with no highlighting.
  • One inch of margin on both sides and across the bottom of every page.
  • A three inch blank band on the top of page one for the Engineer, Auditor and Recorder, and one and a half inches on later pages.

Court and tax authority documents, plats, state and federal documents and anything signed before July 1, 2009 are outside the rule.

sections.h2: What do Fulton County's numbers say about selling a house there?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau counted 42,713 people in 2020 and estimated 41,853 in July 2025, a drop of 2.0 percent. About 80.2 percent of homes are owner occupied, the median value of those homes is $191,000, and the county issued 57 building permits in 2025. Median household income is $72,864 and 94.5 percent of adults finished high school.

Land area is 405 square miles, which gives the county about 105 people per square mile. Most deeds you will see here cover farm parcels, village lots in places like Archbold and Wauseon, or homes in the twelve townships, from Amboy and Chesterfield to Swan Creek and York.

sections.h2: Which Fulton County tax dates matter when a house changes hands?
sections.html:
Fulton County real estate taxes are due in February and July. The Auditor explains that Ohio's tax lien date is January 1 and that taxes are paid a year behind, so taxes paid in 2025 covered tax year 2024 and were based on value as of January 1, 2025.

  • Owner-occupied reduction: it is only for residences and is not applied automatically. Call (419) 337-9200 to sign up.
  • Value complaints: file with the Board of Revision between January 1 and March 31.
  • Payment and mailing address changes: handled by the Treasurer, not the Auditor.

Ask the Fulton County Treasurer for a current balance before closing, and ask the closing agent how taxes are being split between buyer and seller.

faqs.q: Does the Fulton County Recorder charge a transfer tax?
faqs.a: The Recorder's charge is the recording fee. The conveyance fee of $4.00 per $1,000 and the $0.50 per parcel transfer fee are the Auditor's, and Ohio law has the grantor pay the Auditor before the deed is presented for recording.

faqs.q: Can I record a Fulton County deed without going through the Auditor?
faqs.a: Plan on going to the Auditor first. R.C. 322.02 has the grantor pay the county Auditor before the deed is presented to the Recorder, and Fulton County's conveyance standards put legal descriptions through a check at the Auditor, Engineer and Planning offices.

faqs.q: What are the recording hours in Wauseon?
faqs.a: The Recorder is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 am to 4:30 pm at 152 S. Fulton St., Suite 175. The phone number is (419) 337-9232. The Auditor is in the same building, in Suite 165.

faqs.q: What if my deed has the wrong margins or a small font?
faqs.a: It will usually still be recorded, but under R.C. 317.114 the office adds $10 in base fee and $10 in housing trust fee. Court documents, plats, state and federal papers and older instruments are excluded.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a mistake in the value of my Fulton County home?
faqs.a: Call the Auditor's real estate office at (419) 337-9200. A formal complaint goes to the Board of Revision and must be filed between January 1 and March 31, and the Auditor's staff can send or print the form.
